newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-First Merchants Acceptance files for Ch. 11.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-First Merchants Acceptance files for Ch. 11.

text.p: First Merchants Acceptance Corp, which provides financing for used car purchases for consumers with sub-par credit histories, filed for Chapter 11 protection on Friday in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Delaware.
The Deerfield, Ill., company said in April that it had uncovered financial irregularities "involving unauthorized entries" in its records.
First Merchants has said it is in default on a bank loan and on two series of subordinated notes.

First Merchants was unable to finalize a $200 million warehouse credit facility with Greenwich Capital Markets Inc in time to satisfy its bank creditors, First Merchants chief executive William Plamondon said in an interview. He declined to elaborate.
But the company said Friday it had reached an agreement with Ugly Duckling Corp to provide First Merchants with up to $10 million in debtor-in-possession financing.
In a statement, Plamondon said the financing "provides a meaningful opportunity to reorganize, including the resumption of (auto financing) contract purchases."
Until First Merchants releases restated 1996 earnings, it is unclear whether the company will survive without being acquired, one analyst said.
"Until we get a chance to take a look at the financials, it's hard to say at this point," said Daryl Leehaug, a debt analyst who follows the company for Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Co.
First Merchants said in May it expected net earnings for 1996 to be between $0.50 and $0.70 share, compared to the $1.56 a share originally reported.

The bankruptcy filing by First Merchants is the latest sign of trouble for some companies in the sub-prime auto lending market. Those troubles include the announcement in January by Mercury Finance Co, a Lake Forest, Ill., auto financing company, that its profits for the last four years were inflated by accounting irregularities.
Increases in personal bankruptcy filing and overextension of credit by some consumers are hurting the consumer finance industry, especially for sub-prime financers like First Merchants, Leehaug said.
"The sub-prime customer is probably the most prone to get in trouble," Leehaug said.
